analysis.one_liner: Caps federal crop insurance subsidies for big farms and private insurers' guaranteed profits.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan crop insurance reform bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Agriculture Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the federal crop insurance program's cost. It would stop premium subsidies for anyone with income above $250,000, cap taxpayer premium subsidies at $40,000 per person per year, and end subsidies for policies that pay out based on harvest-time market prices [S2][S3]. It would also limit what the private companies that sell crop insurance can be reimbursed for overhead — starting at $900 million a year — cap their rate of return, and let USDA renegotiate its agreement with those companies to save money, while requiring public disclosure of who receives subsidies and how much [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund most crop insurance premiums, would bear less of the cost of subsidies that currently flow without limit, including to very large and wealthy farming operations [S2]. Smaller and mid-sized family farms would compete on less distorted terms once the largest operations lose their uncapped subsidies [S2]. The public would also learn, for the first time in detail, who receives the subsidies and what insurance companies earn from the program [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal premium subsidies for anyone with an average adjusted gross income over $250,000 and caps total subsidy payments at $40,000 per person or entity per year [S2][S3].

Caps reimbursements to private crop insurance companies for administrative and operating costs at $900 million for 2018, adjusted for inflation afterward, and limits their average rate of return to 8.9% of retained premiums [S2][S3].
Ends the budget-neutral requirement for renegotiating the Standard Reinsurance Agreement, allowing USDA to use renegotiation to achieve savings from the private companies [S2][S3].
Requires annual public disclosure of the names of subsidy recipients, the subsidy amounts, indemnity payments, and what each insurance provider earns through the program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private crop insurance companies would lose guaranteed overhead reimbursements and a capped rate of return on the program, and the largest farm operations and wealthiest landowners would lose premium subsidies they currently receive [S2][S3]. Some large commercial farms would face higher out-of-pocket premium costs for additional coverage and harvest-price policies.

drawbacks.text: Farmers use crop insurance as their main protection against drought, flood, and price collapse; scaling back subsidies could raise premiums for some farmers and, critics argue, make the program less affordable and less widely used at exactly the moment of a catastrophic loss [S2].

The crop insurance industry argues that limiting its reimbursements and rate of return could shrink private participation in the program, which the government relies on to deliver coverage nationwide [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's savings come overwhelmingly from the largest subsidy recipients and from guaranteed profits paid to the insurance companies that administer the program, and the family-sized farms that rely most on crop insurance would keep their coverage. The main honest trade-off is that some large commercial farmers would pay more in premiums, and the industry would earn less than its current guaranteed return — real costs, but borne by the program's largest beneficiaries rather than by its intended users.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Flake (R-AZ) introduced the bill on May 3, 2017, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private crop insurance companies that receive guaranteed reimbursements and returns from the program are better off, since the caps and renegotiation powers never took effect. Large farming operations above the proposed income limits also keep their uncapped federal premium subsidies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crop insurers and large subsidized farms

for.name: Sen. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the AFFIRM Act to cut crop insurance subsidies and cap insurers' reimbursements.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the sponsorship bipartisan.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 3, 2017 and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Crop insurance industry
against.role: Private companies that sell and administer federally subsidized crop insurance
against.what_they_did: Faced caps on reimbursements, returns, and renegotiation powers under the bill; the industry has a long record of opposing limits on its program payments.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor, and its fate was committee inaction rather than a party-line vote — no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: These private companies administer the federal program and are reimbursed for administrative and operating costs with guaranteed returns on retained premiums. The bill would cap those reimbursements at $900 million a year, limit their rate of return to 8.9%, and let USDA renegotiate their agreement to save taxpayer money.

Operations with income over $250,000 would lose premium subsidies for additional coverage, and no recipient could receive more than $40,000 in federal subsidies per year. Subsidies for policies pegged to harvest-time market prices would end.

Most farms below the income and per-person caps would keep their subsidized coverage unchanged. The bill's stated aim — reflected in its name — is to redirect support toward family-scale operations by cutting what flows to the largest ones.
